planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, keeping the crown at soil level in full sun and well-drained, humus-rich soil.

directions: Fort Laramie was bred at the University of Wyoming for extreme winter hardiness and continues to be one of the most cold-tolerant everbearing strawberry cultivars available, surviving open winters in zone 3 with minimal mulch protection. Plants produce a moderate spring flush followed by a lighter but steady crop through summer and into fall, with medium, firm, bright-red berries of good dessert quality. Because it tolerates cold so well, it is a reliable choice for northern Plains and mountain-region gardeners where many everbearing varieties struggle to overwinter. Remove blossoms for the first several weeks after spring planting to encourage strong root and crown establishment before fruiting begins.

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and moist, well-drained soil; Totem also performs well as a fall-planted crop in mild maritime climates.

directions: Totem was released by Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada's Pacific research station and became a dominant processing strawberry across the Pacific Northwest for decades, prized for firm, glossy, deep-red fruit that holds up well to freezing and machine harvest. It is a vigorous, high-yielding June-bearer with good resistance to red stele root rot, making it a dependable choice in cool, wet coastal growing regions. Berries are excellent for jam, freezing, and preserves, with slightly less fresh-eating sweetness than dessert-type cultivars. Renovate beds after harvest by mowing foliage and thinning runners to maintain productivity in following seasons.

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained, disease-free soil; avoid replanting into ground that has previously grown strawberries.

directions: Guardian was developed through the Rutgers-USDA strawberry breeding program and was widely planted across the eastern United States for its strong resistance to red stele and verticillium wilt, two soilborne diseases that historically limited strawberry production in humid climates. Plants are vigorous with a spreading habit, producing large, firm, conical berries with good flavor for fresh eating and preserving. Guardian remains a useful choice for gardeners in older strawberry ground or areas with a history of root disease pressure. Mulch with straw over winter in colder zones and renew beds every three to four years as yields decline with plant age.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

planting.note: Set bare-root crowns in early spring in full sun and well-drained soil; mulch heavily with straw before the first hard freeze to protect crowns through harsh winters.

directions: Winona is an early-twentieth-century strawberry cultivar developed in Minnesota and grown for generations in northern home gardens for its exceptional cold hardiness and reliable annual June crop. The medium-sized berries are dark red, aromatic, and well suited to preserving, with a rich, old-fashioned strawberry flavor prized by heirloom growers. Vigorous runnering fills in matted rows quickly, making it well suited to the traditional matted-row growing system used across the northern Plains and upper Midwest. Because it predates most modern disease-resistant breeding, rotate planting sites and use certified disease-free stock to avoid buildup of soilborne pathogens.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Pilgrim is a USDA-bred cranberry cultivar valued for producing some of the largest, deepest-red berries of any commonly grown cultivar, making it popular for fresh-market and specialty use. It ripens later in the season than Stevens, so it is best suited to regions with a long enough fall growing season to fully color before hard freezes. Vines are moderately vigorous with a somewhat more open growth habit than Stevens, requiring the same acidic, saturated bog conditions and coarse sand mulching used for other cranberry plantings. Established vines take three to four years to reach significant production but then bear reliably for many years with minimal maintenance beyond consistent moisture and acidic fertility.
sources: University of Massachusetts Amherst Cranberry Station

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: Early Black is one of the oldest named cranberry cultivars still in cultivation, first selected from wild New England bogs in the mid-1800s and long favored in Massachusetts cranberry growing for its small, very dark, deeply colored fruit and dependable early ripening. Its early harvest window makes it useful in shorter-season northern locations where later-ripening cultivars like Pilgrim may not fully color before frost. Vines are relatively compact and cold hardy, tolerating the harsh winter conditions of traditional New England bogs with proper winter flooding or sanding. As with all cranberries, success depends on maintaining strongly acidic soil, a continuous water source, and a sandy-peat rooting layer.
sources: University of Massachusetts Amherst Cranberry Station

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in spring into strongly acidic, peaty, constantly moist bog soil topped with a sand layer, mimicking commercial cranberry bog conditions.

directions: McFarlin originated in Massachusetts in the 1870s and became the dominant commercial cranberry cultivar across the Pacific Northwest and Wisconsin bogs for much of the twentieth century before being largely replaced by Stevens. It produces large, firm, dark-red berries with good storage quality and was historically one of the parent cultivars used to breed Stevens. Vines are vigorous and productive but somewhat more susceptible to false blossom disease than newer cultivars, so growers should watch for leafhopper vectors and remove infected plants promptly. It remains of interest to home growers and heirloom collectors for its historical significance and reliable regional performance in cooler bog climates.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in very acidic, moist, well-drained soil; Sussi is self-fertile but sets a heavier crop when planted alongside another lingonberry cultivar.

directions: Sussi is a Swedish-bred lingonberry cultivar developed for compact, dense growth and heavy fruit set, making it a popular choice for edible groundcover plantings and container culture. Like other named European lingonberry selections, it produces a smaller summer crop followed by a larger, more concentrated fall crop of small, tart, bright-red berries used in Scandinavian jams and sauces. The low, spreading, evergreen habit tolerates part shade better than most fruiting shrubs, and plants perform best in the same very acidic, humus-rich soil favored by blueberries and other ericaceous plants. Light shearing every few years keeps plantings dense and productive.
